blocks.text: Communication skills • Empathy • Bereavement care • Ethical practice
You are the obstetric doctor caring for a pregnant woman. An ultrasound scan has confirmed intrauterine fetal death (IUFD). You have been asked to inform her and her partner.

items.text: Communicate the diagnosis clearly and compassionately.
Assess the woman's understanding and emotional response.
Allow time for questions and grief.
Explain the immediate next steps without overwhelming her.
Discuss support, consent and follow-up.
Stillbirth following labour.
A diagnosis of a major fetal anomaly.
Severe pre-eclampsia requiring premature delivery.
A poor prognosis for a newborn.
Unexpected maternal complications.

blocks.text: The examiner is assessing how you communicate, not just what information you give.
The SPIKES framework is a useful structure for breaking bad news.
Setting
Provide privacy, sit down, minimise interruptions and ask whom the woman wants present.
Perception
Ask what she understands about the pregnancy, scan or current situation.
Invitation
Ask how much detail she would like to hear now and whether she wants a support person involved.
Knowledge
Give a warning statement, use simple words and explain the confirmed diagnosis clearly.
Empathy
Acknowledge grief, remain present and respond to emotions without rushing.
Strategy and summary
Explain the immediate plan, check understanding and arrange ongoing support.

items.text: Confirm the diagnosis and relevant clinical facts.
Ensure that the scan or investigation has been appropriately interpreted and documented.
Arrange a private, quiet space.
Sit at eye level rather than standing over the patient.
Allow sufficient time and minimise interruptions.
Offer a support person of her choice, if she wishes.
Arrange a nurse, midwife or other appropriate colleague to support her when available.

blocks.text: Do not disclose the news in a crowded ward or where other patients and visitors can overhear.

content_groups.group_title: Step 2: Introduce yourself and establish rapport

blocks.text: Example:

“Good afternoon, Madam. My name is Dr ____. I am one of the doctors looking after you today. I would like to talk with you about the findings from your assessment. Is this a good time for us to speak privately?”
Confirm her identity and ask whether she would like anyone present.

items.text: “Can you tell me what you have been told so far?”
“What were you expecting us to find from the scan?”
“What is your understanding of what has been happening?”

blocks.text: This helps you identify misconceptions and understand how much information she already has.
Prepare the woman for difficult information.

items.text: “I am afraid I have some very sad news.”
“I am sorry, but the results are not what we had hoped for.”
“I need to talk to you about something very difficult.”

blocks.text: Pause briefly before explaining the diagnosis.
For confirmed intrauterine fetal death:
“I am very sorry. The ultrasound scan has shown that your baby's heart is no longer beating. This means that your baby has died.”
Then stop speaking for a moment.
Allow silence. Do not immediately continue with explanations about induction, investigations or delivery unless she is ready to hear them.
Avoid ambiguous phrases such as “we cannot find the baby” or “there is no heartbeat at the moment” when the diagnosis has been confirmed. These can create confusion or false hope.

content_groups.group_title: Step 6: Respond to her emotional reaction

blocks.text: Give her time to react. She may cry, become silent, express anger, ask repeated questions or appear emotionally numb.

items.text: “I am so sorry this has happened.”
“I can see how painful this is for you.”
“Please take your time. I am here with you.”
“Would you like me to stay with you for a while?”
“Is there someone you would like us to contact?”

blocks.text: You do not need to fill every silence.

items.text: “Everything happens for a reason.”
“At least you can have another baby.”
“You are still young.”
“You need to be strong.”
“Do not cry.”
“It was probably God's will.”

blocks.text: These statements may unintentionally minimise her grief or impose beliefs.
If the woman uses religious language, respond respectfully in a way that supports her beliefs without making assumptions.

subsections.subsection_title: 4. Common emotional reactions and how to respond

rows: Offer tissues, remain present and allow silence.
Give time; gently ask whether she would like you to stay or explain more.
Listen calmly, acknowledge the distress and avoid becoming defensive.
Reassure her that she should not assume she caused the death; explain that the cause may not yet be known.
Acknowledge how difficult it is to absorb the news and gently restate confirmed findings.
Asking whether the diagnosis could be wrong
Explain what was confirmed, the steps used to establish the diagnosis and any need for repeat assessment under local protocol.
Assess immediate safety and physical condition; summon appropriate clinical assistance.

blocks.text: Important: Do not assume that an apparently calm response means the woman is unaffected. People grieve differently.

subsections.subsection_title: 5. Explaining what happens next after confirmed fetal death

blocks.text: Once the woman has had time to absorb the news, ask permission to discuss the next steps.
You might say:
“When you feel ready, I would like to explain what we need to do next to look after your health and discuss the options available to you. We can take this one step at a time.”

content_groups.group_title: A. Assess the woman's clinical condition

items.text: Vital signs and general condition.
Vaginal bleeding.
Abdominal pain and uterine tenderness.
Fever or signs of infection.
Hypertension or features of pre-eclampsia.
Relevant obstetric history and gestational age.
Other symptoms suggesting an urgent complication.

blocks.text: If the woman is unstable, has major bleeding, infection or another emergency, urgent treatment takes priority while communication and support continue.
For a clinically stable woman, explain that the team will discuss the safest appropriate method and timing of delivery, taking into account:

items.text: Gestational age.
Maternal health and any complications.
Previous caesarean section or other uterine surgery.
Cervical status and obstetric history.
The woman's preferences and informed consent.
Available expertise and local protocols.

blocks.text: Depending on the clinical circumstances, induction of labour may be offered. Caesarean delivery is not routinely required solely because of fetal death, but individual circumstances may alter the recommended approach.
Avoid giving a rigid management plan before the woman's clinical condition and obstetric history have been assessed.

blocks.title: Depending on the case, investigations may include:

items.text: Full blood count.
Blood group and antibody status.
Coagulation studies if indicated, particularly with prolonged retention or suspected coagulopathy.
Assessment for hypertensive disease, infection or other maternal conditions when clinically indicated.
Placental examination and other investigations to help identify the cause.
Fetal examination, genetic testing or post-mortem examination, where appropriate and with informed consent.

blocks.text: Explain that the cause may not be identified even after a thorough assessment.

content_groups.group_title: D. Discuss seeing and holding the baby

blocks.text: If appropriate, gently explain that the parents may be offered opportunities to see, hold or spend time with their baby.
Example:
“Some parents find it helpful to spend time with their baby, while others prefer not to. There is no right or wrong choice. We can explain the options and support whatever you decide.”
Do not pressure the woman or family into making memories, taking photographs or seeing the baby.

content_groups.group_title: E. Discuss memory-making and cultural or religious preferences

blocks.title: Depending on the woman's wishes and local policy, options may include:

items.text: Photographs.
Hand or foot prints.
A name or keepsake.
Involving a chosen family member or spiritual adviser.
Arrangements for burial or other culturally appropriate practices.

blocks.text: Offer these sensitively, and make it clear that declining is equally acceptable.

content_groups.group_title: F. Discuss the possibility of finding a cause

blocks.text: Say:

“We will review your medical history and discuss investigations that may help us understand why this happened. Sometimes we identify a cause, but sometimes the results do not give us a definite explanation. We will explain the findings to you and arrange follow-up.”
Avoid unsupported claims about the cause, including blaming stress, ordinary activity, food or the mother's behaviour.

subsections.subsection_title: 6. Scenario: breaking the news of a major fetal anomaly

blocks.text: The scan identifies a serious fetal abnormality.

items.text: Confirm that the findings have been appropriately reviewed.
Ask what the woman has been told about the scan.
Give a warning statement.
Explain the abnormality in clear, non-technical language.
Distinguish what is known from what remains uncertain.
Explain the need for specialist assessment where appropriate.
Discuss available options without coercion.
Offer psychological, social, cultural and spiritual support according to her wishes.
Arrange a follow-up discussion rather than expecting her to decide everything immediately.

blocks.text: Example:

“I am sorry, but the scan has shown an abnormality in your baby's development. I know this may be very upsetting. I would like to explain what we have found, what it may mean for your baby and what further assessments or options are available. We can take time to discuss your questions.”
Do not use terms such as “incompatible with life” unless the prognosis has been carefully established and the phrase is appropriate to the situation.
If the baby has died during labour or is delivered without signs of life, communication and bereavement care remain essential.

items.text: Confirm the baby's condition and follow the appropriate neonatal or stillbirth protocol.
Continue appropriate care of the mother, including management of bleeding, pain and other complications.
Inform the mother compassionately and clearly.
Provide privacy and support.
Offer an explanation of what is known, without speculation.
Explain the post-delivery plan and any investigations.
Discuss opportunities to spend time with the baby and available memory-making options.
Arrange bereavement support and follow-up.

blocks.text: Avoid language that suggests the baby was merely a clinical event. Refer to the baby respectfully and use the family's preferred terms where possible.

items.text: Autonomy: Respect the woman's right to participate in decisions.
Beneficence: Act in her best interests.
Non-maleficence: Avoid preventable harm.
Confidentiality: Protect her information and disclose it only as appropriately authorised.
Informed consent: Explain benefits, risks, alternatives and consequences before procedures.
Non-directive counselling: Present options fairly without coercion.

blocks.text: If a partner or relative asks for information before the woman is ready, protect her confidentiality and clarify whom she wants involved, subject to applicable law and immediate safety considerations.
Where urgent treatment is required, explain the situation as fully as the circumstances permit and follow the relevant consent and emergency-care rules.
Bereavement can be associated with severe distress, depression, anxiety and, in some cases, suicidal thoughts.

items.text: Severe agitation or inability to engage.
Hopelessness or extreme self-blame.
Statements suggesting self-harm.
Thoughts of harming others.
Severe confusion, psychosis or inability to remain safe.

blocks.text: If there is concern, ask directly and sensitively about safety and thoughts of self-harm. Arrange urgent mental health assessment when indicated and ensure the woman is not left in an unsafe situation.
Do not pathologise normal grief, but do not overlook a psychiatric emergency.

subsections.subsection_title: 10. Full model OSCE script: confirmed intrauterine fetal death

blocks.text: Example wording for a simulated consultation

“Good morning, Madam. My name is Dr ____, one of the doctors looking after you. I would like to talk with you about the results of your assessment. Would you prefer to speak privately, and is there anyone you would like to have with you?
Before I explain the results, could you tell me what you understand about the scan so far?
I am afraid I have some very sad news.
I am very sorry. The scan has confirmed that your baby's heart is no longer beating. This means that your baby has died.
I am so sorry that you are going through this. I know these words may be very difficult to hear. Please take your time. I am here with you.
[Pause. Allow the woman to respond.]
I can see how painful this is. It is understandable to have many questions, and you do not have to understand or decide everything right now.

At this stage, I cannot tell you exactly why this happened unless we have sufficient evidence. We will review the information available and discuss whether any investigations could help us understand the cause.

Our next priority is your health. We will assess your condition and explain the safest options for delivery and any further care you may need. I will explain the options and answer your questions before any decisions are made, except where emergency treatment is necessary.

You may also choose whether you would like to see or hold your baby, and we can discuss any cultural, religious or family preferences that are important to you. There is no pressure to make that decision immediately.
We will arrange support for you during your admission and after you leave the hospital. You can tell us if you would like a family member, counsellor, midwife or spiritual adviser involved.
What questions or concerns would you like us to address first?”

subsections.subsection_title: 11. Common examiner questions and model answers

blocks.text: Q1. What is the most important principle when breaking bad news?
Communicate honestly and compassionately, in a private setting, using clear language, while allowing time for emotional responses and questions.
Q2. Why use a warning statement?
It prepares the patient emotionally for difficult information and makes the transition to the diagnosis less abrupt.
Q3. Should you tell the patient immediately that the baby has died?
Once the diagnosis is confirmed and the patient is in an appropriate setting, communicate it clearly and sensitively. Avoid unnecessary delays, misleading language or false reassurance.
Q4. What if the woman asks, “Was this my fault?”
Acknowledge the question and reassure her that she should not assume she caused the death. Explain that the cause may be uncertain and that investigations may help clarify it.
Q5. What if the partner becomes angry and accuses the hospital of negligence?

Remain calm, acknowledge the concern, avoid arguing or speculating, explain that the team will review what happened and follow the appropriate complaints or incident-review process. Maintain the woman's safety and confidentiality.
Q6. Should parents be offered the opportunity to see or hold their baby?
Yes, where appropriate, the option should be sensitively offered and explained. The decision belongs to the parents; they should not be pressured.
Q7. What if the woman refuses the recommended management plan?

Assess her understanding, decision-making capacity where relevant, concerns and reasons for refusal. Explain risks, benefits and alternatives, offer further discussion or a second opinion where appropriate, document the discussion and respect an informed decision in accordance with applicable law.
Q8. How do you support the woman after discharge?
Arrange follow-up for physical recovery, review of investigations, discussion of the cause where known, mental health assessment when indicated, and access to bereavement and community support.
Q9. Should you promise that this will never happen again?

No. Provide an individualised assessment of recurrence risk when sufficient information is available. Avoid guarantees and arrange preconception or specialist counselling for a future pregnancy where appropriate.
Q10. What is the difference between empathy and sympathy?
Sympathy expresses concern for someone's suffering. Empathy involves recognising and responding to the person's emotional experience without making assumptions or shifting attention to yourself.

items.text: Delivering the news while standing at the door or in a busy ward.
Using vague expressions such as “something is wrong.”
Continuing to speak without allowing silence.
Offering false reassurance or unsupported explanations.
Saying “at least you can try again.”
Discussing induction or investigations before acknowledging grief.
Assuming the partner should automatically receive all information.
Pressuring parents to see, hold or photograph their baby.
Forgetting maternal physical safety.
Failing to assess immediate psychological risk.
Neglecting follow-up and bereavement support.

blocks.text: Have privacy
Prepare a quiet setting and ask whom the woman wants present.
Explore understanding
Ask what she already knows and what she expects.
Announce clearly
Use a warning statement and plain, unambiguous language.
Respond with empathy
Acknowledge grief, listen and allow silence.
Talk through next steps
Discuss clinical care, choices and support at the woman's pace.
Safety and support
Assess urgent risks, arrange follow-up and offer bereavement support.

Final OSCE tip: In a breaking-bad-news station, the quality of your communication matters more than the amount of information you deliver. Give the diagnosis clearly, pause, acknowledge the person's grief, and discuss the next step only when she is ready or clinical urgency requires it.
